prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and credit limits interact with asset prices to amplify and propagate shocks into credit cycles and macroeconomic fluctuations

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed since round 1. I now propose a two-name B006 award for Kiyotaki and Moore, where before I proposed three names including Gertler. The scientific case for the discovery is unchanged. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) gave macroeconomics a tractable mechanism in which collateral values and credit limits feed on each other, so that small shocks become large and persistent fluctuations. It is nearly thirty years old, was tested by 2007-09, and is now a shared building block of macro, finance and policy models. It is a single, well-bounded mechanism with a clear originating pair. The chair asked whether Gertler's post-accelerator work is a separable achievement, and I tried to answer honestly. His later work on intermediary frictions with Kiyotaki and his work with Karadi on unconventional policy are distinct from the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator. But they are better described as extensions into banks and policy, and the banking and run-type strand sits close to the 2022 prize. I recall these papers from general knowledge and have not checked them. A citation that tried to credit them would need a lot of careful wording to avoid re-recognising adjacent work. A citation for the collateral-amplification mechanism alone does not carry that burden. The pair is therefore the more defensible attribution. It also lets me test B006 on the same standard I apply to the other candidates: a discovery that changed how a whole field reasons, with a clean credit boundary. I do not base this on how many colleagues rank B006 first or name it as an alternative.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is thematic proximity to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. Even with a clean attribution, a committee could judge that macro-finance has recently been recognised and that B006 is less of a new step than a field with no recent prize, such as the B047 candidate. Empirical identification of the specific collateral channel is also mixed. The mechanism's influence on later quantitative and empirical work is clearer than direct validation of the channel. The pair also omits Gertler, whose quantitative and policy-relevant work is influential, and Gilchrist, whose empirical role in the accelerator literature is real. Gertler also appears on the New Keynesian ballot B048. Finally, B047 has an equally clean core and a longer record of use in applied policy. I do not claim that B006 is scientifically decisive over B047. I weigh breadth of use across macro, finance and policy more heavily, and that is a difference of judgement.

responses.point: Hassler's round-1 file prefers Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He ties Gertler's credit to the intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki and to quantitative financial-friction models, not to the accelerator papers that overlap with Bernanke's recognition. He says the committee should state openly that the accelerator credit is partly absorbed. The chair's summary also notes that several members answered his earlier two-name proposal.
responses.response: I anchor on his current three-name file, and I have not tried to answer a position he no longer holds. His distinction is a fair one, and it was my own in round 1. When I try to name the papers that carry Gertler's separate claim, they are the intermediary-frictions chapter with Kiyotaki, the Gertler-Karadi work on unconventional policy, and the Gertler-Kiyotaki banking and liquidity work. Each of these either extends the mechanism into policy or sits near the bank-run themes the 2022 prize addressed. That makes the third name harder to defend than I argued. He has asked that the citation be explicit about this, and I think the cleanest way to be explicit is the pair. I therefore move to Kiyotaki and Moore. I would not oppose a three-name version if he and the committee judge the separable credit sufficient.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B047 first and B006 third. His objection to B006 is that credit has to be drawn around Bernanke's earlier recognition and the 2022 prize, and that this makes it less novel. He treats the choice between B006 and B047 as a legitimate difference in judgement, and he says B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore is the alternative he would most readily support.
responses.response: The two-name version answers the attribution part of his objection, and I welcome his reading that it makes B006 a stronger alternative. We still differ on proximity to the 2022 prize. I would separate the two discoveries. The 2022 prize concerned bank runs, deposit insurance and the cost of banking crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values and credit limits amplify shocks in the real economy. I would be uneasy if the committee applied a strict recent-recognition test to B006 and not to B023's overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes. I agree with him that this is a judgement difference and not a scientific disagreement.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B047 first and proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore for B006. He accepts the work as mature and tested in 2007-09, but he argues that the 2022 overlap makes it less of a new step, and that the evidence on the collateral channel is a weaker base than BLP's decades of applied use. He also notes that Pakes' share in B047 is arguably larger than the other two names'.
responses.response: My change to the pair is the attribution he asked for. I do not move on the newness argument, and I would answer his empirical point in two parts. First, I concede that direct identification of the collateral channel is hard. Second, much of the later empirical work tests downstream predictions of the mechanism, such as how investment responds to changes in the value of collateral. I recall this from general knowledge and have not checked it. I also accept his asymmetry point on Pakes. It does not weaken BLP's attribution, but it does mean B047's trio is less symmetric than it looks, as B006's pair is not. I do not rank it above B047 on merit, and the remaining difference is how heavily to weigh breadth of use.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B047 first. She says that Hassler's two-name framing resolved most of her attribution concern about B006. She still asks whether the collateral channel's record is mainly theoretical validation and broad model adoption, and she would weigh it below a contribution that is both a method and a widely checked empirical practice.
responses.response: I think that is the right question, and the answer is that the two contributions are of different kinds. BLP is an estimation practice that can be re-run and sensitivity-checked in each application. Kiyotaki-Moore is a mechanism that organised a research programme and a way of building models. A mechanism is not validated in the same way. I do not think that makes it less prize-worthy, provided its predictions were tested and it survived 2007-09, but I accept that it lowers the weight of empirical confirmation on the B006 side. This is where we weigh the criteria differently, and I do not claim that it is decisive.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B023 first with Autor, Hanson and Katz, and B006 second. He says he would support the two-name version of B006. He names the Katz-or-Dorn choice, bundling, and overlap with the Goldin and Acemoglu prizes as the unresolved issues in B023, and he lists B006 as the stronger-attributed alternative if B023's attribution cannot be settled.
responses.response: I note that B006's two-name version is his stated fallback, which is useful to know, but I do not count it as support. I agree with his own assessment of B023: the unresolved choice between Katz and Dorn and the bundling of two strands are the main reasons I hold it as an alternative and not as my first choice. I would only ask him a question. If the committee decided that a labour-demand prize should be limited to the trade-shock strand, would he prefer Autor, Dorn and Hanson? I regard that as a cleaner single discovery than the three-name bundle. We also share co-authorship and an institutional tie, which I disclose below, and I have tried not to let it bear on how I weigh his position.

uncertainties: Whether Gertler's separable contributions (intermediary frictions, unconventional policy) are a distinct achievement that the 2022 prize does not cover. I recall the relevant papers from general knowledge and have not checked them. My judgement is that this credit is not clean enough for a third name.
How much weight the committee should give to thematic proximity to the 2022 prize, and whether the same standard would be applied to B023's overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes.
How much the mixed identification of the specific collateral channel should count against B006 relative to the more routinely validated BLP toolkit in B047.
Whether the committee prefers a mechanism-based discovery to a method. I cannot settle this from the shortlist alone.
My assessment of influence, usage and citations rests on general background knowledge and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows long-term co-authorship with John Hassler (chair) and co-authorship with Timo Boppart (co-opted member), and both have stated positions on these candidates. I disclose this without adjudicating it. I am also a long-term co-author of Giovanni Violante, who is credited on B043. That ballot is not in my preferred configuration or my alternatives. None of the credited names on B006, B047 or B023 appears among my listed co-authors, so no recusal-relevant connection to my preferred configuration is apparent from the supplied profile. My own field is heterogeneous-agent macro, which is adjacent to B006, and I have tried to apply the same criteria as for the other fields. I note that I am the committee secretary, and I do not treat that role as evidence about which candidate is better.
